Not one word failed: the land given under Joshua and Solomon

The book of Joshua closes the conquest with a strong summary. The LORD gave Israel all the land he swore to give their fathers; they took possession of it and lived in it. He gave them rest on every side, and not one of all the good promises he had made to Israel failed; all came to pass. Joshua repeats this in his farewell (Joshua 23:14), Solomon in his temple prayer (1 Kings 8:56), and the Levites in Nehemiah's day (Nehemiah 9:7-8).
God promises the land of the Kenites, Hittites, Amorites, Canaanites and others to Abraham's seed.
Joshua records that God gave all the land, gave rest, and that not one good word failed. Joshua 23:14 repeats it.
After the exile the Levites confess that God made a covenant with Abraham to give the land of the Canaanites and others, 'and you have kept your promise, for you are righteous'.
Hebrews says that if Joshua had given the final rest, God would not have spoken later of another day. A Sabbath rest remains for God's people, entered through faith in Christ.
The patriarchs died without receiving the promises in full and desired a better, heavenly country. God has prepared a city for them.

The conquest is dated either to the late fifteenth century BC (from 1 Kings 6:1) or to the thirteenth century; the date and the archaeology of sites such as Jericho, Ai and Hazor remain disputed. The same book that says 'not one word failed' also says that 'very much land' remained to be taken (Joshua 13:1), and Judges 1 lists cities the tribes did not drive out. Under David and Solomon (tenth century BC) the rule of Israel reached from the Euphrates to the border of Egypt (2 Samuel 8:3; 1 Kings 4:21; 2 Chronicles 9:26), and Solomon's feast gathered Israel 'from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of Egypt' (1 Kings 8:65). Nehemiah 9 was prayed after the return from Babylon (mid-fifth century BC), yet still says God had kept his land promise.

This argument reminds believers that God has a record of keeping promises in history. If he kept the land promise to the letter of his own word, he will keep his greater promise of an eternal inheritance (1 Peter 1:3-5). The Christian's rest is not a piece of territory but rest in Christ now and in the new creation later.

Dispensationalists (Walvoord, Pentecost, Fruchtenbaum) answer that Joshua 21:43-45 describes God's faithfulness in giving what the conquest generation could receive, not the final and permanent possession. Joshua 13:1 and Judges 1 show the land was not fully taken, and Solomon ruled vassal kings rather than settling the land with Israel's tribes. Above all, the prophets kept promising the land after Joshua and after Solomon (Jeremiah 32:37-41; Ezekiel 36:24-28; Amos 9:14-15, 'they shall never again be uprooted'), which, they argue, would make no sense if the promise had already been fully discharged.

Fulfilment writers such as Robertson, Burge and Gentry and Wellum answer that Joshua deliberately holds both truths together: God gave all he promised, yet Israel's continued possession depended on faithfulness (Joshua 23:12-16). God's side of the promise was kept; the losses that followed came from covenant breaking, as Deuteronomy 28 had warned. The later prophetic promises of return were fulfilled in the return from Babylon (Ezra 1:1-4; Nehemiah 9:36-37), and their language of permanent security points beyond Canaan, as Hebrews 4 and 11 say. The New Testament never restates the land promise in territorial terms.

Future-camp writers reply that the post-exilic return did not match Amos 9:15 or Ezekiel 37:25 ('forever'), because Israel was uprooted again in AD 70 and AD 135. So, they argue, the prophetic land promises cannot have been fulfilled in 538 BC. Kaiser also notes that the Old Testament repeats the land promise many times as a gift of grace, and that a conditional enjoyment of the land does not make the gift itself conditional.
Exile and return: possession of the land under covenant conditions

Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 warn that if Israel breaks the covenant, they will be scattered among the nations and the land will lie desolate. Yet Leviticus 26:40-45 and Deuteronomy 30:1-6 promise that when the people return to the LORD in exile, he will remember his covenant with the fathers, gather them from the nations, bring them back to the land, and circumcise their hearts so that they love him with all their heart.
If the exiles confess their sin, God will remember his covenant with Jacob, Isaac and Abraham, and will remember the land. He will not reject them utterly.
After curse and scattering, God will restore and gather Israel and bring them into the land, and he will circumcise their hearts.
In the first year of Cyrus, God stirs the king to let the Jews return and rebuild the house of the LORD in Jerusalem.
Caiaphas unknowingly prophesies that Jesus would die for the nation, and not only for the nation but to gather into one the scattered children of God.

Paul reads Deuteronomy 30:12-14 ('the word is near you') as the word of faith in Christ: confess Jesus as Lord and believe God raised him. The heart-circumcision of Deuteronomy 30:6 comes by the Spirit (Romans 2:28-29).
Paul speaks of the coming of the Lord Jesus and 'our being gathered together to him', the final ingathering of God's scattered people.

The curses of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 were carried out in history. Assyria destroyed Samaria and deported the northern tribes in 722 BC (2 Kings 17:5-23). Babylon took Jerusalem in 597 BC (recorded in the Babylonian Chronicle, which dates the capture to 2 Adar, 16 March 597 BC) and destroyed the city and temple in 586 BC (2 Kings 25). Ostraca from Lachish describe the last days before the fall. Cyrus of Persia took Babylon in 539 BC, and his decree (Ezra 1:1-4; 6:3-5) allowed a return in 538 BC; the Cyrus Cylinder, found at Babylon in 1879, records his general policy of restoring displaced peoples and their sanctuaries. 2 Chronicles 36:20-23 links the exile to Jeremiah's seventy years and to the land enjoying its Sabbaths (Leviticus 26:34-35).

The pattern of exile and return teaches that God disciplines his people but does not abandon them. The greatest 'return' is a return of the heart, which God himself works by the Spirit through the gospel. Believers live as people already gathered to Christ, waiting for the final gathering at his coming.

Dispensationalists argue that Deuteronomy 30 describes a final regathering that is followed by national heart-circumcision, and that the return of 538 BC did not meet that standard: most Jews stayed in the dispersion, the returnees remained under foreign rule (Nehemiah 9:36-37), and no national heart-change took place. Ezekiel 36:24-28 puts the regathering before the giving of the new heart. Many dispensationalists, following Walvoord and Fruchtenbaum, therefore see the regathering since the late nineteenth century, and the State of Israel founded in 1948, as at least the beginning of a regathering in unbelief, like the bones gathering before the breath comes in Ezekiel 37:7-10.

Fulfilment writers answer that the Old Testament itself presents the return under Cyrus as the fulfilment of these promises (Ezra 1:1; 2 Chronicles 36:22; Daniel 9:2), and that the 'new heart' promise is applied by the New Testament to the gift of the Spirit at Pentecost (Acts 2:33; 2 Corinthians 3:3-6). Paul reads Deuteronomy 30 itself as speaking of Christ (Romans 10:6-9). Robertson and Burge argue that the 1948 state, founded by a largely secular movement, cannot be the return of Deuteronomy 30, since that return is defined as a return to the LORD 'with all your heart and soul' (Deuteronomy 30:2). The prophetic order is repentance, then return.

Future-camp writers reply that Ezekiel 36-37 clearly has a regathering before spiritual renewal, so a return in unbelief is not ruled out. They also note that Deuteronomy 30:3-5 speaks of gathering from 'all the peoples' and from 'the ends of heaven', which the small return from Babylon and Persia does not match. Progressive dispensationalists are more cautious about 1948 but still expect a future national turning and restoration.
The Davidic covenant: a son on David's throne forever

Through Nathan, God promises David that after his death he will raise up David's offspring and establish his kingdom. This son will build a house for God's name, and God will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. God will be his father and he will be God's son; if he does wrong God will discipline him, but God's steadfast love will not depart from him. David's house and kingdom will be made sure forever, and his throne established forever. Psalms 89:3-4 and Psalms 132:11-12 call this promise a sworn oath.
God promises David an offspring who will build God's house and whose throne will last forever. He will be God's son.
Solomon says God has kept his word: he has risen in David's place, sits on the throne of Israel, and has built the house for the LORD's name.
God has sworn to David that he will establish his offspring forever and build his throne for all generations. Psalms 89:38-51 then laments that the crown has been cast to the ground.
Gabriel says God will give Jesus the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever; of his kingdom there will be no end.

Peter says David knew God had sworn with an oath to seat one of his descendants on his throne, and foresaw the resurrection of the Christ. Jesus, raised and exalted to God's right hand, has been made Lord and Christ.
The kingdom of the world becomes the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he will reign forever and ever.

The Tel Dan Stele, found in fragments in 1993 and 1994 at Tel Dan in northern Israel, is an Aramaic inscription of the ninth century BC, probably set up by Hazael of Damascus. It boasts of victory over a king of Israel and a king of 'the house of David' (bytdwd), the earliest known reference outside the Bible to David's dynasty. Davidic kings ruled in Jerusalem for about four centuries until Zedekiah was blinded and taken to Babylon in 586 BC (2 Kings 25:7). Jehoiachin was released in exile (2 Kings 25:27-30), and Babylonian ration tablets name 'Yaukin, king of the land of Yahud'. After the exile, Zerubbabel of David's line was governor but not king (Haggai 1:1), and the Hasmonean rulers (from 142 BC) and Herod were not Davidic. By the first century, Jewish hope looked for a 'son of David' (Psalms of Solomon 17, first century BC), and the Qumran text 4Q174 reads 2 Samuel 7 as a promise of the 'Branch of David'.

The King believers serve is not a rival to David's line but its promised heir. Jesus reigns now as the risen Son of David at God's right hand, and every believer lives under that reign. Hebrews 1:5 applies 2 Samuel 7:14 ('I will be his father') to Christ, and 2 Corinthians 6:18 extends the father-son language to all believers.

Classic dispensationalists (Walvoord, Pentecost, Ryrie) hold that Christ now sits on his Father's throne in heaven (Revelation 3:21), but that 'the throne of David' is an earthly throne in Jerusalem which he will take at his return (Matthew 25:31; Luke 1:32-33). Luke 1:33 speaks of reigning over 'the house of Jacob', which they read as national Israel. Progressive dispensationalists (Blaising, Bock, Saucy) go further: they agree that Acts 2 shows the Davidic reign has been inaugurated at the ascension, but say its earthly, national phase will be completed in the millennium. Both forms cite Acts 1:6-7, where Jesus does not deny that the kingdom will be restored to Israel.

Fulfilment writers (Riddlebarger, Hoekema, Robertson, Gentry and Wellum) answer that Peter explicitly links the oath to David with the resurrection and ascension: God swore to seat David's descendant on his throne, and David 'foresaw and spoke of the resurrection' (Acts 2:30-31). The throne at God's right hand is therefore the throne of David in its final form. Revelation 3:21 speaks of one shared throne, and Revelation 22:1 calls it 'the throne of God and of the Lamb'. Augustine (City of God 17) already read the promise of an eternal house as fulfilled in Christ and his church, since the Solomonic line failed.

Progressive dispensationalists reply that 'inaugurated' does not mean 'exhausted'. Bock argues that Acts 3:19-21 still speaks of 'times of restoration' that come when Jesus returns, and that Luke-Acts keeps Israel's national hope alive. Classic dispensationalists add that the Old Testament places the Davidic throne in Jerusalem (Jeremiah 33:17; Isaiah 9:7), and that Christ sitting at the right hand is a temporary waiting 'until' (Psalms 110:1).
The king set on Zion and seated at God's right hand

Psalms 2 says God has set his king on Zion, his holy hill. The king is God's son, and God will give him the nations as his inheritance and the ends of the earth as his possession. Psalms 110 has the LORD say to David's Lord: sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool. The LORD will send out his mighty rod from Zion, and he will rule in the midst of his enemies. God has sworn: you are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.
God sets his king on Zion, calls him 'my Son', and promises him the nations and the ends of the earth.
Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, blesses Abram. He joins king and priest in one person, the pattern Psalms 110:4 takes up.
Paul says God has fulfilled the promise to the fathers by raising Jesus, as Psalms 2 says: 'You are my Son; today I have begotten you.'
Peter quotes Psalms 110:1. David did not ascend to heaven; Jesus did, and God has made him Lord and Christ.
God raised Christ and seated him at his right hand far above every rule and authority, put all things under his feet, and gave him as head over all things to the church.
Christ must reign until God has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy destroyed is death; then comes the end, when he hands the kingdom to the Father.

Psalms 2 and 110 were probably royal psalms used at the enthronement of Davidic kings in Jerusalem; Psalms 110 is attributed to David in its heading. Psalms 110:1 is the Old Testament text most often quoted or echoed in the New Testament. Jesus used it to ask how David's son could be David's Lord (Matthew 22:41-46). Before Christianity, Jewish writers already read Psalms 2 of the coming Messiah: Psalms of Solomon 17 uses the 'rod of iron' image, and the Qumran Florilegium (4Q174) links Psalms 2 with 2 Samuel 7. Melchizedek is also a heavenly figure in the Qumran text 11Q13 (11QMelchizedek).

The reign of Christ is not only a future hope; he is seated and ruling now. The church's mission goes out from the risen King, who has 'all authority in heaven and on earth' (Matthew 28:18). Because he is also priest forever, believers have a permanent high priest who intercedes for them (Hebrews 7:23-25).

Dispensationalists stress the word 'until' in Psalms 110:1. Christ now sits at the Father's right hand and waits; the active rule 'from Zion' over enemies (Psalms 110:2) and the striking of the nations with a rod of iron (Psalms 2:9; Revelation 19:15) take place when he returns. Historic premillennialists such as Ladd agree that Christ reigns now in heaven, but read Revelation 20:4-6 and 1 Corinthians 15:23-24 as allowing an interval between his coming and 'the end' in which his reign is displayed on earth.

Fulfilment writers (Hoekema, Riddlebarger, Beale) answer that 1 Corinthians 15:25 says Christ 'must reign until' all enemies are under his feet, so the time of sitting is the time of reigning. Paul places the defeat of death, the last enemy, at the resurrection when Christ comes (1 Corinthians 15:23-26, 54-55), leaving no room for a later age in which death still occurs (compare Isaiah 65:20, which premillennialists apply to the millennium). Hebrews 10:12-13 says Christ sat down after one sacrifice for sins, waiting until his enemies are made his footstool, which presents his priestly and royal work as complete in principle now.

Premillennialists reply that 'then the end' (1 Corinthians 15:24) uses a word ('then', eita) that can allow an interval, just as there has been an interval of nearly two thousand years between 'Christ the firstfruits' and 'those who are Christ's at his coming' (1 Corinthians 15:23). They argue that Revelation 20 supplies that interval. Classic dispensationalists add that Psalms 110:2 locates the rule 'from Zion' and so on earth.
The righteous Branch: 'The LORD is our righteousness'

God promises to raise up for David a righteous Branch, who will reign as king, act wisely, and do justice and righteousness in the land. In his days Judah will be saved and Israel will dwell securely, and his name will be 'The LORD is our righteousness'. Jeremiah 33:14-18 repeats the promise and adds that David will never lack a man on the throne of Israel, and the Levitical priests will never lack a man to offer burnt offerings.
God will raise a righteous Branch for David, a wise king who does justice. His name will be 'The LORD is our righteousness'.
After the exile, Joshua the high priest and his companions are a sign: God will bring his servant the Branch.
God's Son was descended from David according to the flesh and declared Son of God in power by the resurrection.
Christ Jesus became for believers wisdom from God, righteousness, sanctification and redemption. The Branch's name becomes the believer's gift (2 Corinthians 5:21).
Jesus calls himself 'the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star'.

Jeremiah spoke this oracle in the last years of Judah, probably under Zedekiah (597-586 BC), whose throne name means 'The LORD is my righteousness'. The promised king's name 'The LORD is our righteousness' contrasts with the failed king and the 'shepherds' condemned in Jeremiah 23:1-2. Zedekiah was the last Davidic king to reign in Jerusalem; he was captured near Jericho and taken to Riblah in 586 BC (Jeremiah 39:4-7). The 'Branch' image is shared with Isaiah 11:1 (a shoot from the stump of Jesse) and Zechariah 3:8 and 6:12. Jeremiah 33:14-26 is missing from the Greek Septuagint, a fact discussed by textual critics.

Believers are declared righteous because the King is righteous and gives his righteousness to them. The Branch's name is now the confession of every Christian: our righteousness is the LORD himself, in Christ. His wise and just reign is also the pattern for how his people live.

Dispensationalists note that the Branch will 'do justice and righteousness in the land' and that in his days 'Israel will dwell securely' (Jeremiah 23:6), followed by a new exodus 'from the north country' back to 'their own land' (Jeremiah 23:7-8). For Walvoord and Pentecost this describes Christ's earthly reign over a regathered nation, which has not yet happened. Jeremiah 33:17 promises a Davidic king on 'the throne of the house of Israel', which they read as a literal throne in Jerusalem in the millennium.

Fulfilment writers point out that Jeremiah 33:18 promises in the same breath that Levitical priests will never lack a man to offer burnt offerings 'continually'. If verse 17 must be literal, verse 18 must be too, but Hebrews teaches that Levitical sacrifice has ended in Christ (Hebrews 7:11-12; 10:11-18). The better reading, Robertson and Gentry and Wellum argue, is that both promises are fulfilled in Christ, who is both David's son and the eternal priest. The new covenant of Jeremiah 31:31-34, given to 'the house of Israel and the house of Judah', is quoted in Hebrews 8:8-12 as fulfilled in Christ's ministry to the church.

Some dispensationalists (Hullinger, Whitcomb) reply that the sacrifices of Jeremiah 33 and Ezekiel 40-48 can be literal in the millennium as memorials or for ceremonial cleansing, not atonement. Progressive dispensationalists (Saucy, Bock) reply that Hebrews applies the new covenant to the church as an inaugurated fulfilment, without cancelling Jeremiah 31:35-37, where Israel's continuance as a nation is as sure as the sun and moon.
The fallen tent of David rebuilt, and the nations called by God's name

Amos ends his book of judgment with hope. In that day God will raise up the fallen booth (tent) of David, repair its breaches, and rebuild it as in the days of old, so that they may possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations that are called by God's name. The book closes with abundant harvests and Israel planted in its land, never again to be uprooted (Amos 9:13-15).
God will rebuild David's fallen booth, and all the nations called by his name will be included in its rule.
Zechariah praises God for raising up a horn of salvation for us 'in the house of his servant David'.

At the Jerusalem council James says Peter's report of Gentiles believing agrees with the prophets, and quotes Amos 9:11-12 (in a form close to the Greek Old Testament): God rebuilds David's tent so that the rest of mankind, all the Gentiles called by his name, may seek the Lord.
Gentiles are now fellow citizens with the saints and members of God's household, built together into a holy temple and a dwelling place for God by the Spirit.
The dwelling place ('tabernacle', the same Greek word family as the 'tent' of David in Acts 15:16) of God is with people, and he will dwell with them.

Amos prophesied in the days of Uzziah of Judah and Jeroboam II of Israel, 'two years before the earthquake' (Amos 1:1), around 760 BC; destruction layers at Hazor and other sites are often linked to a large mid-eighth-century earthquake, which Zechariah 14:5 also remembers. Speaking to a prosperous northern kingdom, Amos already called David's house a 'fallen booth', looking ahead to its collapse in 586 BC. Before Christianity, the Qumran community read Amos 9:11 of the coming Branch of David (4Q174) and of the books of the Law (the Damascus Document, CD VII). The Jerusalem council of Acts 15 is usually dated around AD 48-50. James quotes a text close to the Septuagint, which reads 'the rest of men' (Hebrew adam) where the Hebrew has 'Edom'.

Gentile believers today are part of the rebuilt house of David. James used this text to settle that Gentiles do not need to become Jews (by circumcision) to belong to God's people. The church, Jew and Gentile together, is the place where David's Son now rules and where God dwells.

Classic dispensationalists, following Scofield and Walvoord, read James's opening words 'After this I will return' (Acts 15:16) as an order of events: first God takes out from the Gentiles a people for his name (Acts 15:14, the church age), and after that Christ returns to rebuild David's tent in the millennium. James only claims that the prophets 'agree' with Gentile salvation, not that Amos is fulfilled now. Progressive dispensationalists such as Bock, and Walter Kaiser in a well-known 1977 article, accept that Acts 15 sees an initial fulfilment now, but hold that Amos 9:14-15 still promises Israel's permanent planting in its land.

Fulfilment writers (Robertson, Beale, Holwerda) answer that James's whole argument requires that the rebuilding has begun: the inclusion of Gentiles 'called by my name' is the purpose of the rebuilt tent, so if Gentiles are being included now, the tent is standing now. 'After this I will return' is not in Amos and is probably drawn from texts such as Jeremiah 12:15 or Hosea 3:5 to frame the quotation, not to insert the church age. Richard Bauckham argues that the 'tent of David' was read in Jewish exegesis as the eschatological temple, which James identifies with the community of Jewish and Gentile believers.

Dispensationalists reply that James's point is agreement in principle: God always planned to save Gentiles as Gentiles, which the church shows. This does not prove that the national promises of Amos 9:14-15 ('I will plant them on their land, and they shall never again be uprooted') have been met, especially since Israel was uprooted in AD 70 and AD 135.
Ezekiel's temple, the returning glory and the river of life

In Ezekiel 40-48 the prophet is shown a vast temple with exact measurements. The glory of the God of Israel, which had left the temple before its destruction (Ezekiel 10-11), returns from the east and fills the house; God says this is the place of his throne, where he will dwell among Israel forever (Ezekiel 43:1-7). A river flows from the temple, making the Dead Sea fresh and feeding trees whose leaves are for healing (Ezekiel 47:1-12). The land is divided among the twelve tribes in parallel strips, and the city is named 'The LORD is there' (Ezekiel 48:35).
The glory returns to the temple, and God says he will dwell in the midst of Israel forever.
The returned exiles finish the second temple in the sixth year of Darius and dedicate it with joy. It does not follow Ezekiel's plan, and no return of the glory is recorded.
Jesus cries out that rivers of living water will flow from within whoever believes in him. John explains that he means the Spirit.
Paul says 'we are the temple of the living God' and quotes God's promise to dwell among his people and be their God (Leviticus 26:12; Ezekiel 37:27).
John sees no temple in the new Jerusalem, for the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb are its temple.
The river of the water of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb, with the tree of life whose leaves are for the healing of the nations, as in Ezekiel 47:12.

Ezekiel 40:1 dates the vision to the twenty-fifth year of the exile, fourteen years after Jerusalem fell, which is 573 BC. The prophet was among the exiles taken to Babylon with Jehoiachin in 597 BC. The second temple, begun under Zerubbabel in 536 BC and completed in 515 BC (Ezra 3:8; 6:15), did not follow Ezekiel's design, and Herod's rebuilding (begun c. 20/19 BC) did not either. Ezekiel's temple therefore has never been built. Jewish interpreters noticed difficulties with it; the Babylonian Talmud (Shabbat 13b) says that Hananiah ben Hezekiah worked to reconcile Ezekiel's rules with the Law of Moses.

God's purpose is to dwell with his people, and that purpose is met now in Christ and in the church as God's temple by the Spirit. The river of Ezekiel 47 is the life of the Spirit flowing out through believers to the world. The healing of the nations in Ezekiel 47:12 is the goal of Christian mission and the hope of the new creation.

Dispensationalists such as Feinberg, Pentecost, Walvoord and Hullinger argue that Ezekiel's detailed measurements, gates, chambers and tribal borders demand a literal, future, millennial temple. They answer the problem of animal sacrifices in two main ways: as memorials looking back to the cross (like the Lord's Supper), or, in Hullinger's view, as offerings for ceremonial purity needed because the holy presence of God dwells on an earth still affected by sin. The temple was never built after the exile, so they argue it must still be future.

Fulfilment writers (Beale, Block, Hoekema, Robertson) answer that the vision is shown 'in visions of God' on 'a very high mountain' (Ezekiel 40:2), like the symbolic visions earlier in the book. Its sacrifices are said to 'make atonement' (Ezekiel 45:15, 17), the prince offers a sin offering for himself (Ezekiel 45:22), and uncircumcised foreigners are barred (Ezekiel 44:9); a literal return to these after Christ would conflict with Hebrews 10:18 ('there is no longer any offering for sin') and Ephesians 2:14. Revelation 21-22 takes up Ezekiel's images (the high mountain, the measured city, the twelve gates, the river and trees) and fulfils them in a city that has no temple because God and the Lamb are its temple.

Dispensationalists reply that the Hebrew word for atonement (kipper) can mean ceremonial cleansing, as it does for objects such as the altar (Ezekiel 43:20, 26), not only forgiveness of sin. They also argue that the order of Revelation 20-22 allows Ezekiel's temple in the millennium (Revelation 20) and no temple in the eternal state (Revelation 21:22). Block, though not a dispensationalist, agrees that Ezekiel's vision is ideological rather than a building plan; dispensationalists see this as a concession that the text is not being read on its own terms.
The latter glory of this house will be greater than the former

To the discouraged builders of the second temple, God says that in a little while he will once more shake the heavens and the earth, the sea and the dry land, and all nations. The treasures (or 'the desire', KJV) of all nations will come in, and he will fill this house with glory. The silver and gold are his. The latter glory of this house will be greater than the former, and in this place he will give peace.
God will shake heaven, earth and nations, fill the house with glory, and make its latter glory greater than Solomon's.
When the foundation of the second temple is laid, the old men who had seen Solomon's temple weep aloud while others shout for joy.
The infant Jesus is brought into the temple. Simeon calls him God's salvation, a light for revelation to the Gentiles and the glory of God's people Israel.
Jesus says, 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.' John explains that he spoke of the temple of his body.
Hebrews quotes Haggai 2:6 on the final shaking and says believers are receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken.
The kings of the earth bring their glory into the new Jerusalem, and the glory and honour of the nations are brought into it.

Haggai 2:1 dates this word to the twenty-first day of the seventh month in the second year of Darius I, about 17 October 520 BC. The returned exiles had laid the foundation in 536 BC (Ezra 3:8-13) but stopped for about sixteen years; work resumed in 520 BC and the temple was completed in 515 BC (Ezra 6:15). Later Jewish tradition (Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 21b) lists things missing from the second temple, including the ark and the Shekinah glory. Herod the Great rebuilt and enlarged the second temple from his eighteenth year (c. 20/19 BC, Josephus, Antiquities 15.380), and John 2:20 notes it had been under construction for forty-six years when Jesus spoke. Rabbinic writers held that the 'latter glory' was fulfilled in Herod's grand building or in the temple's longer duration; Christian writers held it was fulfilled when the Lord came to his temple (Malachi 3:1).
